question: Why must a nurse consider a patient's cultural background during dietary counselling?

options.A: To legally satisfy federal hospital documentation requirements for nutrition
options.B: To ensure the recommended meal plan fits the patient's lifestyle and is realistic to follow
options.C: To calculate the exact body mass index of family members living at home
options.D: To completely eliminate traditional foods that might interfere with modern medicine

explanation: A diet plan only works if the patient will actually eat the food. Respecting culture ensures the advice is practical and acceptable. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T002#GNS227_U7_T002_h1)

question: How can a nurse tell the difference between moulding and caput succedaneum during a physical assessment?

options.A: Caput only happens in breech presentations, while moulding only happens in head-first births
options.B: Moulding disappears within minutes of birth, but caput lasts for several months
options.C: Moulding involves bone overlapping, whereas caput is soft swelling that can cross over suture lines
options.D: Caput feels hard like solid bone, whereas moulding feels soft like fluid

explanation: Caput is soft fluid swelling that crosses suture lines, while moulding is the shifting of the hard skull bones themselves. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T14#GNS121_U6_T14_h5)

question: A patient with a head injury seems stable. Why must you keep monitoring them closely over the next few days?

options.A: Complications often develop hours or days after the primary injury
options.B: Hospital policies require discharges within 48 hours
options.C: Patients usually fake their symptoms to get more attention
options.D: Medications stop working completely after the first day

explanation: Brain swelling takes time to build up. A patient looking fine right now can take a sudden turn for the worse later, so constant watch is key!

question: Which imaging test uses contrast dye and X-rays to clearly view the inside of the uterus and fallopian tubes?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Saline infusion sonohysterography
options.C: Hysterosalpingography
options.D: Abdominal CT scan

explanation: Correct! Hysterosalpingography (HSG) combines 'hystero' (uterus), 'salpingo' (tubes), and 'graphy' (imaging) using dye to see if the tubes are open.

question: What is a well-known long-term issue for people who survive Lassa fever?

options.A: Loss of vision
options.B: Chronic kidney failure
options.C: Deafness
options.D: Permanent limb paralysis

explanation: Hearing loss is quite common after recovering from Lassa fever, and unfortunately, it can sometimes be permanent.

question: What is the primary job of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

options.A: Securing big money grants for labs
options.B: Writing nursing textbooks
options.C: Marketing new drugs to hospitals
options.D: Protecting the rights and safety of human research participants

explanation: Spot on! The IRB acts as a safety shield to ensure human subjects are treated ethically and safely.

question: What is the main goal of giving CPR to a patient?

options.A: To clear a blocked airway using forced abdominal thrusts
options.B: To cure the underlying cause of a sudden heart attack
options.C: To manually circulate oxygenated blood to vital organs
options.D: To restart a stopped heart using manual electric shocks

explanation: You're doing great! Remember that CPR doesn't usually restart the heart on its own. Instead, your hands act as a pump to keep oxygen flowing to the brain and heart until help arrives.

question: Which lab values must a nurse check before a patient receives gadolinium contrast dye for an MRI?

options.A: Fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c
options.B: Kidney function tests like creatinine and BUN
options.C: Liver enzymes and total protein counts
options.D: Complete blood count and platelet levels

explanation: Contrast dye is filtered through the kidneys, so poor kidney function can lead to dangerous complications like nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why is IEC considered a preventive approach instead of a curative one?

options.A: It focuses on changing health behaviors before sickness happens
options.B: It replaces the need for doctors and nurses in rural areas
options.C: It provides free medicines to patients inside the hospital ward
options.D: It diagnoses infectious diseases using laboratory testing

explanation: Spot on! IEC is all about stopping health problems before they even start by educating communities, rather than waiting to treat people after they fall sick.

question: What is the best position to place a patient in before you start feeding them?

options.A: Trendelenburg position with feet elevated higher than the head
options.B: High Fowler's position or 90 degrees upright in a chair
options.C: Semi-Fowler's position at a gentle 30-degree angle
options.D: Flat on the back with a small pillow under the neck

explanation: Sitting upright uses gravity to help food go down smoothly and, most importantly, keeps the airway safe from choking.

question: Which anti-nausea medication is commonly given as a skin patch behind the ear for motion sickness?

options.A: Metoclopramide
options.B: Aprepitant
options.C: Scopolamine
options.D: Ondansetron

explanation: Spot on! Scopolamine is a popular anticholinergic patch that travels through the skin to prevent motion sickness during travel. Great clinical fact to remember!

question: What key tip should you give a patient who just got a 7-day course of oral antibiotics?

options.A: Share extra pills with family members who catch the same illness
options.B: Finish all 7 days of medicine even if you feel completely better
options.C: Double the next dose if you forget to take one on time
options.D: Stop taking the capsules as soon as your fever goes away

explanation: You're getting the hang of this! Feeling better doesn't mean the germs are all gone. Finish the full 7 days to wipe them out completely.

question: Why do we need to eat water-soluble vitamins more often than fat-soluble ones?

options.A: They are destroyed immediately by stomach acid during digestion.
options.B: They turn into toxic waste products if they stay in the bloodstream.
options.C: They are burned up instantly for energy during physical exercise.
options.D: They wash out easily and cannot be stored in large amounts in the body.

explanation: Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in body fluids, and whatever your body doesn't use is passed out in your urine. That's why you need a fresh supply regularly!

question: Which emergency during the third stage of labor requires an immediate hospital transfer?

options.A: Mild postpartum fatigue
options.B: Normal placental separation
options.C: Transient shivering after birth
options.D: Severe postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Heavy bleeding after delivery can quickly become life-threatening. Stop the bleeding and get the mother to the hospital fast!

question: Why is randomization so important when assigning patients to study groups?

options.A: It gives every participant an equal chance of ending up in any group
options.B: It ensures that only the oldest patients get the new treatment
options.C: It makes the research paper shorter to write
options.D: It allows the nurse to choose which patient needs the therapy most

explanation: Randomization spreads patient differences evenly across groups, preventing researcher bias from messing up the final results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: How did nursing education in Nigeria change after the country gained independence in 1960?

options.A: Universities began offering degree programs in nursing science
options.B: Training was moved entirely out of hospitals into military camps
options.C: All foreign-trained nurses were banned from practicing locally
options.D: Traditional herbalism completely replaced western pharmacology

explanation: After independence, nursing grew rapidly as a profession, and Nigerian universities started offering degree courses to elevate nurse training.

question: Why is preventing hypothermia so important when stabilizing a trauma victim?

options.A: Standard rescue stretchers only function properly in warm weather
options.B: Hypothermia causes patients to become overly aggressive with staff
options.C: Warm patients require fewer intravenous fluids during transport
options.D: Cold exposure worsens blood clotting problems and increases mortality

explanation: You're doing awesome. Trauma patients lose body heat fast, and cold temperatures stop blood from clotting properly, making bleeding much harder to control.

question: What usually happens to a hospital when its budget is slashed during an economic recession?

options.A: An immediate surplus of advanced surgical equipment
options.B: Shorter working hours and increased pay for all staff
options.C: Shortages of essential drugs and basic medical supplies
options.D: Free accommodation provided for every admitted patient

explanation: When hospital budgets drop, everyday items like gloves, drugs, and basic lab reagents become scarce very quickly.

question: What is the main way the poliovirus spreads in a community?

options.A: Inhalation of respiratory droplets from sneezing
options.B: Direct skin contact with an infected skin rash
options.C: Vector-borne transmission via mosquito bites
options.D: Fecal-oral route through contaminated water or food

explanation: Spot on! Polio spreads mainly through the fecal-oral route, usually when people consume food or water contaminated with infected waste.

question: How do checklists help prevent unfair or biased observations in a study?

options.A: By allowing the researcher to change the questions daily
options.B: By evaluating every participant using the same criteria
options.C: By removing human judgment completely from the process
options.D: By hiding the study goals from the clinical staff

explanation: When everyone is measured against the exact same standard, personal opinions won't sway your results. Fair and square!

question: Why do low-income communities often experience higher rates of endemic waterborne diseases?

options.A: Overcrowded schools running multiple shifts daily
options.B: Lack of proper sanitation infrastructure and safe drinking water
options.C: Higher consumption of locally brewed herbal beverages
options.D: Greater resistance of local bacteria to standard antibiotics

explanation: Without clean water systems and proper sewage disposal, water sources easily become contaminated with disease-causing microorganisms. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which part of the peripheral nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement?

options.A: Somatic nervous system
options.B: Parasympathetic division
options.C: Sympathetic division
options.D: Autonomic nervous system

explanation: The somatic system is responsible for conscious control over skeletal muscles. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why does the nurse need to keep track of the exact sizes of the dilators used during the procedure?

options.A: To determine how long the patient must stay NPO afterward
options.B: To prevent the doctor from using metal instruments twice
options.C: To monitor the progressive widening of the stricture safely
options.D: To bill the hospital pharmacy for disposable plastic items

explanation: Doctors stretch the tissue step-by-step, going up in size very gradually. Tracking the sizes helps the team avoid jumping up in diameter too fast, which protects the patient from tearing.

question: Why is 30 degrees Celsius not considered twice as warm as 15 degrees Celsius?

options.A: Because Celsius measurements have uneven gaps between numbers
options.B: Because the scale lacks a true absolute zero point
options.C: Because thermal energy cannot be measured numerically
options.D: Because temperature is actually measured on a nominal scale

explanation: Without a true zero point where temperature completely disappears, you can't multiply or say something has 'twice as much' heat.

question: What key element is missing from a vague aim statement like 'we will improve patient safety'?

options.A: Detailed medical diagnoses for every patient
options.B: A complete history of past nursing errors
options.C: The signatures of the hospital board of directors
options.D: Specific targets, a timeline, and the target patient group

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! Without knowing how much change, by when, and for whom, a team can't measure success.

question: A patient has severe liver disease. Which part of drug processing will most likely be affected?

options.A: Metabolism
options.B: Excretion
options.C: Dissolution
options.D: Absorption

explanation: Spot on! The liver is our main metabolic factory where drugs are broken down and processed.

question: Why should a research design make it easy for others to repeat the study?

options.A: So other researchers can repeat the study and check the results
options.B: So the original author can publish the exact same paper twice
options.C: To reduce the cost of printing physical textbooks
options.D: To prevent patients from participating in future studies

explanation: That's right! When other nurses can repeat your study and get similar results, it proves the findings are trustworthy and strong.

question: What is the single most reliable way to monitor daily changes in a patient's fluid balance?

options.A: Daily body weight measurement
options.B: Counting how many times they eat
options.C: Measuring abdominal girth
options.D: Checking skin turgor on the arm

explanation: One liter of fluid weighs one kilogram, making daily weights the fastest and most accurate indicator of gain or loss. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T7#GNS123_U3_T7_h6)

question: Which ethical principle guides a nurse's duty to act in the best interest of their psychiatric patient?

options.A: Veracity
options.B: Beneficence
options.C: Paternalism
options.D: Autonomy

explanation: Beneficence is all about doing good and taking positive actions to care for and protect your patients. It's at the heart of nursing ethics!

question: What is the main physiological purpose of dietary proteins in the body?

options.A: Maintaining rapid nerve conduction and fluid balance
options.B: Tissue growth, hormone synthesis, and immune defense
options.C: Providing a dense energy reserve for long-term fasting
options.D: Acting as a solvent for fat-soluble vitamins

explanation: Proteins are made of amino acids that build and repair tissues, create vital enzymes and hormones, and support immune function. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T001#GNS227_U2_T001_h2)

question: Why are community-based approaches important alongside clinic visits?

options.A: They allow nurses to fine men who refuse to visit the clinic.
options.B: They replace the need for any hospitals or clinics in rural areas.
options.C: They reach men within their own social environments and cultural comfort zones.
options.D: They ensure that women stay indoors during pregnancy.

explanation: Taking health talks to town halls and local spots engages men right where they naturally gather. Fantastic job!

question: What term describes an increase in the total number of muscle fibers during fetal development?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Atrophy
options.D: Hypertrophy

explanation: Hyperplasia is simply the multiplication of cells that increases the absolute count of muscle fibers before birth. You're doing amazing!

question: What is the main reason labs use differential growth media?

options.A: To completely kill off all unwanted bacteria in a clinical sample
options.B: To preserve the live bacterial sample in the refrigerator for many months
options.C: To increase the total physical size of individual bacterial cells for easy viewing
options.D: To tell different bacteria apart by showing color changes from their chemical reactions

explanation: Well done! Differential media use color changes right on the Petri dish so lab techs can easily spot which bacteria is which.

question: What is the very first step a nurse should take when entering a new community for health mobilisation?

options.A: Administering vaccines without telling anyone first
options.B: Visiting local leaders to gain entry and approval
options.C: Building a clinic fence using community donations
options.D: Conducting a written examination for all adults

explanation: Community entry respects local hierarchy and customs by seeking permission and blessing from traditional or civic authorities first. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which spinal nerve roots give rise to the nerves of the pelvic floor?

options.A: T10 to L1
options.B: S2 to S4
options.C: L1 to L3
options.D: C1 to C3

explanation: Correct! Remember 'S2, 3, 4 keeps the pelvic floor off the floor!' A handy little trick for your exams.

question: A patient started on strong opioid analgesics for cancer pain is most at risk for which common side effect that requires proactive nursing intervention?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: Severe constipation
options.C: Chronic diarrhea
options.D: Persistent insomnia

explanation: Opioids significantly slow down bowel motility, meaning almost every patient starting regular opioids needs preventative laxatives prescribed alongside them. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T13#GNS321_U4_T13_h2)

question: What is the main goal of community programs that prevent adolescent substance use?

options.A: Isolating teenagers from their peer groups completely
options.B: Stopping substance abuse before experimentation begins
options.C: Imposing harsh criminal punishments on drug users
options.D: Closing down all local pharmacies and stores

explanation: You nailed it! Prevention is all about stepping in early with healthy coping skills and support before drug use ever starts.

question: Why is it so important for a nurse to check a pregnant patient's diet early on?

options.A: It determines the exact date of conception
options.B: It replaces the need for standard laboratory blood tests
options.C: It allows for the early identification and correction of nutrient deficits
options.D: It stops gestational diabetes from ever developing

explanation: Spotting nutritional gaps early helps you stop issues like tiredness or baby growth delays before they become serious. Great nursing insight!

question: What is the proper term for professional negligence committed by a healthcare provider?

options.A: Insubordination
options.B: Defamation
options.C: Battery
options.D: Malpractice

explanation: Malpractice simply means professional negligence—when a healthcare provider fails to meet the expected standard of care and a patient gets hurt. You will master these terms easily!

question: How does constraint-induced movement therapy help a client with weakness on one side of their body?

options.A: It builds bulk muscle strength in the weak arm through heavy weightlifting.
options.B: It forces the brain to use the weak side by restricting the strong side.
options.C: It permanently immobilizes the strong side to prevent accidental injury.
options.D: It eliminates pain in the joints by keeping the limbs completely still.

explanation: By gently resting or blocking the good arm, we trick and encourage the brain to wake up and practice using the weaker side, boosting neuroplasticity!

question: A nurse researcher wants to prove that a new wound care protocol prevents infections better than the old method without relying on messy old records. Which study design should be chosen?

options.A: Prospective design
options.B: Cross-sectional snapshot
options.C: Case-control past analysis
options.D: Retrospective chart review

explanation: A prospective design allows the researcher to implement the protocol today and record infection rates moving forward with high accuracy. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h3)

question: How do microbes mainly get around from place to place in the air?

options.A: Chemical attraction to vehicle exhaust
options.B: Magnetic pulls from the earth's core
options.C: Self-propulsion using microscopic flagella
options.D: Wind currents and air turbulence

explanation: You got it! Microbes can't fly on their own, so they completely rely on wind and moving air to carry them.

question: How is quality assurance different from quality control?

options.A: Quality assurance lowers patient numbers, while quality control increases them
options.B: Quality assurance is only done by doctors, while nurses handle quality control
options.C: Quality assurance deals with finances, while quality control deals with medications
options.D: Quality assurance focuses on preventing errors, while quality control detects defects after care is given

explanation: Think of it this way: assurance looks at the whole process beforehand to stop mistakes, whereas control checks things after the work is already finished to spot what went wrong.

question: What is the normal environment of the vagina in a healthy woman of childbearing age?

options.A: Acidic
options.B: Neutral
options.C: Alkaline
options.D: Variable

explanation: You're right! Friendly bacteria called lactobacilli keep the vagina acidic to protect it from bad germs and infections.

question: What is the main purpose of monitoring during a community health project?

options.A: Continuous tracking of activities to ensure they stay on schedule
options.B: Punishing staff members who arrive late to the clinic
options.C: Waiting until the very end of the project to check patient files
options.D: Increasing the financial budget halfway through the program

explanation: You got it! Monitoring happens while the project is running so we can catch delays or issues early and fix them.

question: Why do healthcare providers check a patient's level of insight during diagnosis?

options.A: It helps determine if the patient recognizes their beliefs as irrational
options.B: It shows if the family history contains genetic markers for depression
options.C: It proves whether the patient is physically capable of walking unaided
options.D: It measures the exact chemical levels of serotonin in the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! Checking insight lets us know if the patient realizes their fears are over-the-top, which helps shape how we plan their care.

question: A pregnant patient asks if she can safely drink fresh, unpasteurized goat milk. What is your best response as a nurse?

options.A: Yes, as long as the goat appears healthy and clean
options.B: No, because raw milk may contain dangerous Listeria or Brucella
options.C: No, but only because raw milk causes severe lactose intolerance
options.D: Yes, because goat milk naturally lacks all human pathogens

explanation: You're doing great! Pregnant women should always avoid raw milk because it can harbor nasty infections like Listeria and Brucella that harm both mother and baby.

question: What is the main difference between macronutrients and micronutrients?

options.A: If they come from plant or animal sources
options.B: How fast they dissolve in the bloodstream
options.C: The total amount the body requires daily
options.D: Whether they can provide energy to the body

explanation: You got it! Macro means large (needed in grams), while micro means small (needed in tiny milligram or microgram amounts).

question: What should you do if a patient cannot remember the names of their home medications?

options.A: Disregard home drugs and start fresh hospital drugs
options.B: Guess the medications based on their visible disease symptoms
options.C: Scold the patient for being careless with their health
options.D: Ask the patient or family to bring all medicine containers to the clinic

explanation: Having them bring their actual bottles or sachets gives you exact, reliable data when memory fails. Simple and practical!

question: Why do we count water as a nutrient even though it gives us zero calories?

options.A: It breaks down into simple sugars inside the stomach lining
options.B: It is essential for life, acting as a medium for all metabolic reactions
options.C: It stimulates the production of digestive enzymes in the pancreas
options.D: It converts directly into structural tissue during growth phases

explanation: Correct! A nutrient is anything needed for survival and body chemistry—it doesn't have to provide energy to be vital.

question: How does a nurse best show public health advocacy regarding breathing disorders?

options.A: Doing deep lung biopsies in local health clinics
options.B: Isolating every single person with a seasonal flu
options.C: Supporting policies that cut down air pollution and tobacco use
options.D: Prescribing strong bronchodilators to people in the neighborhood

explanation: Advocacy goes beyond the hospital bedside. Nurses advocate by supporting healthier environments, clean air policies, and community tobacco control.

question: Why is clearing stagnant water around your home such a powerful public health habit?

options.A: It removes the breeding sites where mosquitoes lay their eggs
options.B: It prevents houseflies from finding garbage to eat
options.C: It stops tsetse flies from resting in tall grass
options.D: It kills adult blackflies instantly

explanation: No standing water means mosquitoes lose their nursery! Draining puddles and old tires is one of the easiest ways to prevent malaria in our communities.

question: What is the main goal of routine childhood immunization programs?

options.A: To stimulate active immunity against specific dangerous pathogens
options.B: To treat children who are already sick with chronic illnesses
options.C: To replace nutritional supplements in the diet
options.D: To eliminate the need for handwashing and sanitation

explanation: Vaccines train a child's immune system to fight off dangerous germs ahead of time, building a protective shield without making them sick!

question: If you are posted as a nurse to a new displacement camp, what major environmental challenge should you expect?

options.A: Immediate surplus of specialized surgical equipment
options.B: Excessive availability of modern private housing
options.C: Complete absence of any communicable diseases
options.D: Overcrowding and limited access to clean water

explanation: New camps often spring up overnight, leading to heavy crowding and tough living conditions. As nurses, anticipating clean water shortages helps us prevent disease outbreaks!

question: Which hormone tells the gallbladder to release stored bile?

options.A: Secretin
options.B: Gastrin
options.C: Cholecystokinin (CCK)
options.D: Insulin

explanation: When fats and proteins hit your small intestine, it releases CCK, which signals the gallbladder to squeeze and release bile.

question: Why do public health teams evaluate immunization services?

options.A: To reduce the total number of required clinic visits
options.B: To increase the market price of new vaccines
options.C: To measure program performance and safety
options.D: To punish staff who miss vaccination targets

explanation: Evaluation is simply our way of checking if our vaccination programs are running safely and truly protecting our communities. You've got this!

question: Why do infection control teams need members from many different hospital departments?

options.A: Because infection prevention touches every area of patient care and facility operations
options.B: Because cleaning staff are the only ones trained to use chemical disinfectants
options.C: Because labor laws require equal representation from all hospital departments
options.D: Because doctors alone cannot write prescriptions for powerful antibiotics

explanation: Exactly! Stopping germs takes teamwork—from clinicians and lab scientists to admin staff—because infection risks can pop up anywhere.

question: At a hot outdoor concert, a nurse notices attendees feeling dizzy, nauseous, and sweating heavily. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Immediately discharge them from the venue without further assessment
options.B: Administer powerful intravenous antibiotics to all affected individuals
options.C: Move them to a shaded cooling area and provide oral rehydration
options.D: Advise them to continue dancing until the concert concludes

explanation: Classic signs of heat exhaustion! Getting them out of the sun and giving fluids right away stops it from turning into heatstroke.

question: What happens to systemic blood pressure when arterioles undergo widespread vasoconstriction?

options.A: Blood pressure drops because the vessel walls become too stretched
options.B: Blood pressure remains unchanged because cardiac output compensates completely
options.C: Blood pressure drops because blood flow through the vessels speeds up
options.D: Blood pressure increases because vascular resistance rises

explanation: Constricting arterioles narrows their lumen, which increases resistance and raises the overall pressure within the arterial system. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is a major consequence of gender-based power imbalances in many communities?

options.A: Reduced autonomy for women regarding their health and reproductive decisions
options.B: Elimination of all barriers preventing men from accessing mental healthcare
options.C: Universal access to high-quality healthcare for gender-diverse people
options.D: Equal distribution of household resources among all family members

explanation: When power is concentrated unequally, women often lack the decision-making power needed to protect their own health and well-being. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T1#GNS312_U4_T1_h7)

question: How should a nurse respond when a teen shares a wild cultural myth about birth control?

options.A: Laugh to show how ridiculous the rumor sounds to professionals
options.B: Scold the teenager for believing such foolish stories in public
options.C: Gently validate their concern and provide accurate, simple facts
options.D: Ignore the statement entirely and prescribe whatever is easiest

explanation: Always meet patients with kindness, not judgment. Listening first helps you correct misinformation effectively.

question: What should you do if you notice fresh, bright red bleeding from the rectum after a washout?

options.A: Report the finding to the physician immediately
options.B: Document it as a completely normal expected result
options.C: Administer a stronger oral laxative dose to the patient
options.D: Wait twenty-four hours to see if it stops on its own

explanation: Bright red blood means there might be a small injury or tear in the lining. Always let the doctor know right away so it can be checked.

question: What is a common danger when researchers use very long or complex checklists during busy ward shifts?

options.A: Observer fatigue leading to rushed or guessed answers
options.B: Automatic rejection of the study by the ethics committee
options.C: Immediate breakdown of hospital computer networks
options.D: Patients refusing to take their prescribed medications

explanation: Keep it concise! When tools are too long and staff are tired, they lose focus and might just start guessing.

question: Why do we test changes on a small scale during the 'Do' phase of a project?

options.A: To test an idea safely on a small group before changing the whole hospital
options.B: To hide the project from management until it's finished
options.C: To punish nurses who don't follow guidelines
options.D: To avoid collecting numbers and rely only on guesses

explanation: Exactly! Small tests let you catch flaws early without putting patients or staff at risk across the entire facility. Smart nursing in action!

question: Why is a personalized nutrition chat usually better than just handing a patient a printed meal plan?

options.A: It guarantees rapid weight loss without any effort
options.B: It replaces the need for medical checkups entirely
options.C: It costs nothing for the healthcare facility to provide
options.D: It takes into account the patient's personal lifestyle and culture

explanation: Spot on! Generic meal plans often fail because they ignore how people actually live and eat at home. Tailoring your advice to their culture and routine makes all the difference.

question: Why don't we pull back (aspirate) on the plunger anymore for routine subcutaneous shots like insulin?

options.A: It makes the medication completely inactive in the syringe
options.B: It increases the risk of the needle breaking in the skin
options.C: It causes unnecessary tissue trauma and increases bruising
options.D: It causes the plunger to stick permanently inside the barrel

explanation: Modern practice shows that the chance of hitting a vessel here is tiny. Pulling back just causes extra discomfort and bruising for no real benefit.

question: Why do community health nurses need to understand vital statistics?

options.A: To diagnose rare diseases in individual patients
options.B: To calculate daily hospital meal portions
options.C: To see the health trends of the entire community
options.D: To manage the financial payroll of the ward

explanation: Looking at population numbers helps nurses understand broader health patterns rather than just focusing on one sick person at a time. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h1)

question: How can community health nurses best fight social stigma against disability?

options.A: By ignoring cultural beliefs entirely without discussion
options.B: By focusing solely on medication management in clinics
options.C: Through patient advocacy and public health education
options.D: By keeping affected individuals hidden safely at home

explanation: Brilliant! Education and speaking up help clear away harmful myths, replacing fear with inclusion and understanding.

question: A patient tells you they are a transgender man who is married to a man. What does this demonstrate?

options.A: Gender identity always determines a person's romantic preferences
options.B: Sexual orientation changes automatically after a social transition
options.C: Gender identity and sexual orientation are completely separate concepts
options.D: Transgender individuals cannot experience same-sex attraction

explanation: This scenario highlights that a person's internal sense of gender does not dictate who they are romantically attracted to. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T1#GNS312_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why do malnutrition and chronic infections often trap people in a vicious cycle?

options.A: Vitamins can only be absorbed if a person has a chronic parasite.
options.B: Infections cause permanent brain damage that stops people from eating.
options.C: Malnutrition weakens immunity, and infections worsen nutritional status.
options.D: Malnutrition prevents antibiotics from working inside the stomach.

explanation: You've got it! Poor nutrition lowers your defense against sickness, and being sick robs your body of nutrients—each one feeds the other.

question: What is the main job of antiemetic medications?

options.A: Lowering high blood glucose levels in diabetes
options.B: Preventing or relieving nausea and vomiting
options.C: Stimulating regular bowel movements
options.D: Reducing excess stomach acid production

explanation: Antiemetics target the vomiting center in the brain or gut to help settle an upset stomach and stop vomiting.

question: What does an "out-of-pocket" payment mean in healthcare?

options.A: Reimbursement given to nurses for buying personal uniforms
options.B: Grants donated by foreign organizations to rural clinics
options.C: Monthly salary deductions paid automatically by the government
options.D: Direct cash payment made by patients at the point of receiving service

explanation: Spot on! Out-of-pocket means the patient is dipping straight into their own wallet to pay for drugs, tests, and consultations right there at the hospital.

question: A nurse records a patient's daily urine output as 1000 mL, which is exactly double yesterday's output. What scale makes this math possible?

options.A: Ratio scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Ordinal scale
options.D: Nominal scale

explanation: Because urine output has a true zero (0 mL means absolutely no urine), you can safely make direct comparisons like 'twice as much'.

question: During a building collapse with dozens of victims, a patient with severe, fatal injuries gets an expectant (black) tag. Why do we do this?

options.A: Because nurses are not legally allowed to touch trauma patients outdoors
options.B: To preserve scarce medical supplies for victims who have a better chance of survival
options.C: Because minor injuries always take legal precedence over head trauma
options.D: To punish the patient for not wearing safety equipment

explanation: This is one of the hardest parts of nursing, but when supplies are limited, we must focus our efforts where we can genuinely save lives.

question: Why are normal losses from breathing and light sweating called insensible fluid losses?

options.A: They only happen when the patient is unconscious
options.B: They do not affect the body's overall fluid balance
options.C: They cannot be measured directly with standard equipment
options.D: They are completely harmless to the human body

explanation: Insensible losses evaporate continuously into the air and through the skin without leaving a pool of liquid to measure. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h4)

question: If a patient catches a really strong (virulent) strain of bacteria, what are they most likely to experience?

options.A: A much longer and milder incubation window
options.B: Zero replication inside the lymphatic system
options.C: Complete immunity without ever showing symptoms
options.D: A shorter incubation period with faster symptom onset

explanation: You got it! Highly virulent bugs cause tissue damage rapidly, meaning symptoms pop up much faster.

question: What does a right-skewed histogram usually tell us about hospital wait times?

options.A: The data collection process had errors and must be discarded
options.B: Most patients wait a very long time, with almost no quick visits
options.C: Every single patient waits the exact same amount of time
options.D: Most patients wait a short time, while a few wait a very long time

explanation: A right-skew has a bunch of tall bars on the left for quick waits, and a long tail stretching right for those rare, super-long waits.

question: Why do clinical nurses need to team up with environmental health officers?

options.A: To replace the need for community health education programs
options.B: To ensure that hospital beds are only filled with surgical patients
options.C: To effectively address both the infected patient and the environmental reservoir
options.D: To reduce the cost of purchasing pharmaceutical drugs for clinics

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Treating the sick patient in the ward isn't enough if we don't clean up the environmental source causing the sickness outside.

question: Why is 'Disturbed Body Image' a common nursing diagnosis for conditions like Cushing's syndrome?

options.A: Visible physical changes like weight gain and facial swelling alter a person's appearance.
options.B: Hormonal imbalances cause permanent memory loss and confusion.
options.C: Severe muscle weakness prevents the patient from looking in a mirror.
options.D: Patients lose their sense of hearing and balance due to inner ear fluid shifts.

explanation: Spot on. Cushing's brings noticeable body changes, like round 'moon facies' and weight shifts, which can be really tough on a patient's self-esteem.

question: A patient undergoing fertility testing shares that she feels deeply sad and worthless. What is the best first thing for a nurse to do?

options.A: Assure her that medical treatments work on the first try for almost everyone
options.B: Tell her that adoption is a very easy alternative to consider right away
options.C: Advise her to stop thinking about pregnancy so her hormones will normalize
options.D: Acknowledge her emotional pain and offer a supportive, non-judgmental space to talk

explanation: You nailed it! Validating her deep emotional pain builds essential trust and shows true compassionate nursing care. Keep up the wonderful work!

question: What do we call the mild mood swings and crying spells many women feel in the first week after birth?

options.A: Baby blues
options.B: Puerperal fever
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Postpartum psychosis

explanation: Spot on! The 'baby blues' are very common and normal due to sudden hormone shifts. They usually pass on their own within two weeks with a little love and support.

question: What is the main benefit of storing energy as fats (lipids) instead of carbohydrates?

options.A: Fats provide more than double the energy per gram
options.B: Fats do not require oxygen for complete breakdown
options.C: Lipids dissolve easily in water for rapid transport
options.D: Lipids can be converted directly into red blood cells

explanation: Fats are super energy-dense! They pack more than twice the energy punch per gram compared to carbs, making them a very compact way to store backup fuel.

question: Why is it smart to call the receiving hospital on the phone before sending an emergency patient?

options.A: To confirm the exact home address of the ambulance driver
options.B: To ask the doctor on duty for permission to use their hospital ambulance
options.C: To ensure the receiving team can prepare equipment and space for the patient
options.D: To negotiate the medical bills before the patient arrives at the gate

explanation: A quick heads-up phone call lets the hospital prep a bed, oxygen, or blood products before the ambulance even rolls through their gates.

question: If household incomes in a community suddenly increase, what change in healthcare use are we likely to see?

options.A: An increase in the uptake of elective and preventive health services
options.B: A total cessation of visits to traditional local healers
options.C: No alteration in how residents access local health clinics
options.D: A sharp decrease in the number of emergency room admissions

explanation: Spot on! When people have more money in their pockets, they can finally afford wellness checks, vitamins, and elective care before emergencies happen.

question: What is the typical chemical structure of a dietary fat (triglyceride)?

options.A: Four interlocking carbon rings with a side chain
options.B: One nitrogen group attached to a central carbon ring
options.C: Two sugar rings joined by a strong glycosidic bond
options.D: One glycerol molecule attached to three fatty acid tails

explanation: Think of it like a central backbone (glycerol) holding onto three fatty acid tails—hence 'tri-glyceride'. Great job!

question: What part of a sterile field package is always considered contaminated?

options.A: The exact center of the drape
options.B: The items placed inside the wrapper
options.C: The outer one-inch border
options.D: The bottom surface resting on the table

explanation: The outer edge touches non-sterile surfaces during opening, so the outer one-inch margin is treated as contaminated. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h5)

question: What should you do if you notice a clinical policy on your ward is outdated or confusing?

options.A: Change the national health laws to match personal preference
options.B: Report the gap through official institutional channels
options.C: Throw away all printed copies of the hospital rulebook
options.D: Keep the information secret from all other staff members

explanation: Using official reporting channels helps management fix and update policies safely without encouraging risky shortcuts on the ward.

question: When must you wear a surgical mask while working in the surgical suite?

options.A: In the unrestricted zone when greeting incoming patients and families
options.B: Whenever staff members feel unwell or have a mild cough
options.C: In the restricted zone where sterile supplies and procedures are located
options.D: Only when the surgeon is actively making an incision on the patient

explanation: Masks protect the sterile field from mouth and nose droplets, so they are mandatory inside the restricted zone at all times.

question: Which type of cell division is responsible for producing sperm and egg cells?

options.A: Meiosis
options.B: Osmosis
options.C: Binary fission
options.D: Mitosis

explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half, creating specialized reproductive cells needed for sexual reproduction. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h5)

question: What are the three main pillars of health financing?

options.A: Raising, pooling, and purchasing
options.B: Planning, staffing, and evaluating
options.C: Insuring, billing, and auditing
options.D: Prescribing, dispensing, and storing

explanation: Think of health financing as collecting funds (raising), putting them together to share risks (pooling), and paying for care (purchasing). You've got this!

question: A nurse leaves the ward during a busy shift to run personal errands miles away and causes an accident. Who carries the blame?

options.A: The state nursing council
options.B: The hospital administration
options.C: The chief medical director
options.D: The nurse personally

explanation: Because the nurse was way out of bounds doing personal things away from work, the hospital escapes vicarious liability, leaving the nurse to face it alone.

question: What is the medical term for excessive thirst experienced by a client with high blood sugar?

options.A: Proteinuria
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polyphagia
options.D: Polydipsia

explanation: Polydipsia is the medical word for extreme thirst, which happens because the body loses a lot of water through frequent urination. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h4)

question: How do retinal arterioles typically appear compared to retinal venules during an ophthalmoscopic exam?

options.A: Arterioles are darker red and wider than venules
options.B: Arterioles are brighter red and narrower than venules
options.C: Arterioles and venules look completely identical in color
options.D: Arterioles have no visible blood flow inside them

explanation: Arterioles carry oxygenated blood and appear narrower and brighter red than the wider, darker venules running alongside them. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T8#GNS221_U2_T8_h2)

question: What are the two main mechanisms that move an egg through the fallopian tube?

options.A: Blood pressure and gravity
options.B: Ligament pulling and fluid diffusion
options.C: Cilia sweeping and muscular peristalsis
options.D: Ovarian suction and uterine contractions

explanation: Hair-like cilia on the lining cells and wave-like muscle contractions work together to push the egg along. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of establishing a just culture in a healthcare facility?

options.A: Protecting the hospital administration from ever facing malpractice lawsuits
options.B: Encouraging staff to report errors openly without fear of unfair punishment
options.C: Eliminating all human error completely through strict daily monitoring
options.D: Ensuring that every nurse who makes a mistake loses their license

explanation: A just culture creates a safe environment where staff feel confident reporting mistakes so the facility can learn from them. [learn more](GST319_U6_T1#GST319_U6_T1_h2)

question: Why must a nurse always clean an instrument before disinfecting it?

options.A: To sterilize the equipment without using heat or gas
options.B: To dry the medical instrument so it does not rust
options.C: To remove organic matter that can block chemical disinfectants
options.D: To instantly kill all bacterial spores present on the surface

explanation: Think of dirt or dried blood as a shield for germs! Cleaning washes away that organic barrier so your disinfectant can actually reach and kill the bacteria.

question: What common side effect should you warn a patient about when they start taking an SGLT2 inhibitor?

options.A: Severe low blood sugar episodes occurring mostly during the night
options.B: Genital fungal infections due to increased glucose in the urine
options.C: Permanent kidney failure caused by excessive strain on the nephrons
options.D: Rapid and dangerous weight gain from fluid retention in the legs

explanation: Well done! Since there is extra sugar in the urine, it creates a sweet environment where fungi love to grow, increasing the risk of local infections.

question: What is the main job of the Olfactory nerve (Cranial Nerve I)?

options.A: Smell
options.B: Hearing
options.C: Vision
options.D: Taste

explanation: Spot on! Cranial Nerve I is our olfactory nerve, carrying messages about different smells from our nose up to the brain.

question: What is personal invulnerability in the context of adolescent psychology?

options.A: An advanced ability to resist peer pressure in all situations
options.B: The physical resistance to common sexually transmitted infections
options.C: A clinical diagnosis of complete emotional numbness
options.D: The belief that bad outcomes happen to others but never to oneself

explanation: Teens often think they are immune to pregnancy and infections, which leads them to take unnecessary risks with unprotected sex. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T9#GNS312_U3_T9_h3)

question: Why do doctors often choose synergistic drug combinations?

options.A: To ensure patients spend less money at the pharmacy
options.B: To make medication administration schedules much simpler
options.C: To completely eliminate all possibilities of adverse drug reactions
options.D: To achieve a stronger therapeutic outcome than single drugs provide

explanation: Combining agents synergistically lets clinicians tackle stubborn health conditions much more effectively by boosting overall treatment power.

question: How do civil service rules and professional nursing acts work together for a public sector nurse?

options.A: Civil service rules completely replace professional nursing laws upon employment
options.B: The nurse must obey both administrative civil service rules and professional health regulations
options.C: The constitution prevents nurses from being held accountable to civil service guidelines
options.D: Professional council regulations only apply to private hospital nursing staff

explanation: As a public sector nurse, you answer to two bosses in a way: your administrative employers (civil service rules) and your profession (the nursing council).

question: Which of these medications would you NOT give directly into the heart muscle for routine pain relief?

options.A: Calcium chloride
options.B: Epinephrine
options.C: Morphine sulfate
options.D: Atropine

explanation: Morphine is a pain reliever (analgesic), not a cardiac arrest drug. It is never poked straight into the heart muscle!

question: What are the two main parts of the human immune system?

options.A: Primary and secondary defense
options.B: Innate and adaptive immunity
options.C: Cellular and humoral barriers
options.D: Active and passive antibodies

explanation: Great job! The immune system has two main teams: innate immunity (the fast, born-with-it guards) and adaptive immunity (the smart specialists that learn to fight specific germs over time). You've got this!

question: Which of these is NOT a normal symptom of the postpartum blues?

options.A: Temporary fatigue from broken sleep patterns
options.B: Mild mood swings and unexpected crying spells
options.C: Severe delusions and thoughts of harming the infant
options.D: Feeling slightly overwhelmed by new responsibilities

explanation: Crying spells and feeling overwhelmed are totally normal as hormones shift. However, delusions or thoughts of hurting the baby are never normal blues—they are signs of a severe emergency like postpartum psychosis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h6)

question: What is the main goal of Behavioural Change Communication (BCC) in public health?

options.A: Distributing medical supplies to rural clinics
options.B: Diagnosing rare tropical infectious diseases
options.C: Writing detailed hospital administration reports
options.D: Promoting positive and sustainable health habits

explanation: You've got this! BCC is all about using interactive ways to help people and communities build healthy habits that actually last.

question: What is the main benefit of using an infusion pump instead of a normal gravity IV line?

options.A: It warms the intravenous fluid before it enters the vein
options.B: It completely removes the need to monitor the IV site
options.C: It delivers fluids at a precise and controlled rate
options.D: It prevents all forms of air embolisms automatically

explanation: Spot on! Infusion pumps give us exact control over how fast fluids run, which is much safer and more reliable than just relying on gravity.

question: Which of these is a clear example of a 'direct cost' in nursing?

options.A: Salary of the chief executive officer
options.B: Depreciation of the hospital building
options.C: Wages of the bedside nurse providing patient care
options.D: Monthly electricity bill for the entire hospital

explanation: Direct costs are expenses you can pin directly to a specific patient, like the actual hands-on nursing time spent caring for them.

question: What is a key characteristic of direct ophthalmoscopy?

options.A: It produces an inverted image that must be flipped mentally
options.B: It requires a heavy head-mounted light source worn by the examiner
options.C: It provides an upright, magnified view of a small retinal area
options.D: It gives a complete wide-angle view of the entire peripheral retina

explanation: Direct ophthalmoscopy uses a handy device to give an upright image magnified roughly 15 times, though it covers a narrower field than indirect methods. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T8#GNS221_U2_T8_h3)
